architectural_implications.after: An instrumentation layer emits agent/tool/retriever spans; evaluators are authored against concrete trace fields and dataset columns.
architectural_implications.before: Evaluators written speculatively against assumed outputs, with prompt strings as the only artifact.
architectural_implications.consequence: Eval infrastructure becomes downstream of the observability schema; changing span attributes is a breaking change for evaluators.
architectural_implications.observation: Trace capture must precede and constrain eval authoring, since criteria are derived from observed spans.

architectural_implications.after: One evaluator definition promoted from dev dataset evaluation to continuous online evaluation over production traces.
architectural_implications.before: Ad-hoc grading logic embedded per-experiment, unable to run on live traffic.
architectural_implications.consequence: Need versioning and schema-stability guarantees for evaluator definitions, similar to model or migration versioning.
architectural_implications.observation: Evaluators become parameterized artifacts (prompt template + variable bindings) that move from playground to dataset backtests to online production runs.

architectural_implications.after: Prompt/model changes must clear eval pass-rate thresholds before deploy.
architectural_implications.before: Prompt changes shipped on subjective review; regressions discovered by users.
architectural_implications.consequence: Eval suites acquire the same maintenance burden and flakiness risk as test suites, including judge nondeterminism as a new source of CI flake.
architectural_implications.observation: Quality gates in CI are treated as the deployment boundary for prompts and agent graphs.

architectural_implications.after: Per-step grading over tool calls, retrievers, and intermediate model spans with localized failure labels.
architectural_implications.before: A single overall quality score per conversation.
architectural_implications.consequence: Storage, cost, and compute for evaluation scale with trace depth, not request count — a new capacity-planning axis.
architectural_implications.observation: Failure attribution shifts from root span to sub-span granularity in agent graphs.

article_ideas.angle: Architecture dependency ordering: tracing to trace inspection to criteria to judge execution to online monitoring.
article_ideas.based_on: You need observability and traces before you can write effective evals.
article_ideas.thesis: Evaluation criteria are derived from observed agent spans, so trace instrumentation and span schema are the real foundation of an eval program; teams that author judges before inspecting traces grade imagined failure modes.
article_ideas.title: Your Evals Are Only as Good as Your Traces

article_ideas.angle: Failure attribution in agent traces and why span-level grading turns a score into a fix.
article_ideas.based_on: a single root-level output grade is under-diagnostic
article_ideas.thesis: Root-level output evals are under-diagnostic for agents because upstream tool and retriever errors cascade; actionable evals must attach to spans and localize failures to the step that can be fixed.
article_ideas.title: Stop Grading Only the Final Answer

article_ideas.angle: Modularity applied to grader design, with per-dimension pass-rate tracking.
article_ideas.thesis: Atomic single-dimension judges with concrete pass/fail bullets are more auditable and regressable than multi-quality rubrics; vague criteria are a rubric failure mode, not a prompt-writing inconvenience.
article_ideas.title: One Judge, One Question

article_ideas.angle: Splitting detection from diagnosis, with annotation as a first-class signal source.
article_ideas.based_on: Metrics and evals answer different questions
article_ideas.thesis: Production telemetry needs two outputs: anomaly detection from metrics and failure-mode characterization from evals; collapsing them into one dashboard loses the diagnosis step.
article_ideas.title: Metrics Detect, Evals Diagnose

connections.relationship: Evaluation depends on span-level instrumentation as its evidence source; eval schema is coupled to trace schema.
Applies the modularity principle from software design to grader design, enabling per-dimension regression tracking.

connections.connects_to: typed bindings between evaluator and dataset schema
connections.relationship: The binding layer is the silent-failure surface; schema changes break evaluators the way API changes break clients.

connections.concept: CI quality gates on pass-rate thresholds
connections.relationship: Evals act as the regression test suite for artifacts edited in natural language.
Propagation of upstream tool/retriever errors motivates sub-span grading and per-step failure labels.

evidence_quotes.text: You need observability and traces before you can write effective evals.
Agent traces involve trees of agents, tools, and model calls where errors cascade.

core_insights.generalization: For any non-deterministic multi-step system, the debugging substrate (traces/spans) must exist and be readable before automated grading can be specified; observability is a precondition for evaluation, not a sibling capability.
core_insights.insight: Evaluation of agents is ordered after observability: you must first capture and read multi-step traces (agent trees, tool calls, retriever spans) before you can author a meaningful evaluator. Traces are the evidence substrate from which eval criteria are derived, not a parallel concern.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It forces a dependency ordering in the platform stack: instrumentation/tracing → trace inspection → criteria authoring → judge execution → production monitoring. Teams that build judges before inspecting real traces will write rubrics for imagined failure modes.

evidence_quotes.text: Single LLM calls have one input and output span.
Agent traces involve trees of agents, tools, and model calls where errors cascade.

core_insights.generalization: In composed pipelines, evaluate at the granularity where the fault can be repaired; terminal-output metrics are observability of symptoms, not of causes.
core_insights.insight: Error cascades in agent traces mean a single root-level output grade is under-diagnostic: failures originate in intermediate LLM calls, tool calls, or retriever steps and propagate. Evaluation therefore has to be able to attach to spans/sub-steps rather than only final responses.
core_insights.why_it_matters: A passing root-output eval can mask a broken retriever or a wrong tool call that happened to be compensated downstream; a failing root eval gives no localization. Span-level grading is what turns a score into an actionable fix.

evidence_quotes.text: Judge one quality per eval for LLM-as-a-judge.
Vague criteria fail; concrete criteria succeed.

core_insights.generalization: Apply single-responsibility decomposition to graders as you would to functions: one judge, one decision boundary, one pass-rate metric.
core_insights.insight: Judge design should be atomic: one quality dimension per LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, with each criterion expressed as concrete pass/fail bullets. Vague descriptors are explicitly treated as a failure mode of the rubric itself.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Decomposing into single-dimension judges makes the judge prompt's decision surface narrow and auditable, and lets each dimension be tracked, regressed, and fixed independently — a modularity argument for the eval suite itself.

evidence_quotes.text: Your criteria become your eval prompt.
Variable mapping connects eval inputs and outputs to exact dataset columns.

core_insights.generalization: Treat evaluators as parameterized programs over a schema (prompt template + input bindings), not as prose rubrics; the binding layer is where most silent eval bugs live.
core_insights.insight: Criteria are operationalized by translating them into an eval prompt plus explicit variable mapping from dataset columns to the judge's inputs/outputs — i.e., the rubric is compiled into a prompt template plus a typed binding to the trace/dataset schema.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Variable mapping is the interface contract between the eval and the logged data; getting it wrong silently grades the wrong field. It also makes the evaluator portable from playground to dataset runs to production traffic.

evidence_quotes.text: Decision models for fast/cheap yes/no tests; code checks for JSON structure validation and regex; Rouge/BLEU for text matching.
Different eval types serve different stages from development to production.

core_insights.generalization: Build a tiered grading stack (deterministic → small model → large model → human) and route each check to the lowest tier that is sound for it.
core_insights.insight: Eval methods form a cost/capability portfolio selected by stage and question type: decision models for cheap fast binary checks, deterministic code/logic checks for structural properties (JSON validity, regex), text-similarity metrics like Rouge/BLEU for matching, LLM-as-a-judge for semantic qualities, human annotation and user feedback for judgment calibration — with online evals continuing in production.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Choosing the cheapest evaluator that can answer the question avoids paying LLM-judge latency and cost on things a regex or classifier can settle, while reserving semantic judges for what only they can grade.

evidence_quotes.text: Metrics tell you something is broken, but evals tell you what the failure mode is.
Every stakeholder evaluates the agent, not just engineers.

core_insights.generalization: In production ML systems, split the telemetry into anomaly detection and failure-mode characterization, and treat domain-expert labeling as a first-class signal source feeding the loop.
core_insights.insight: Metrics and evals answer different questions: metrics detect that something broke, evals characterize what the failure mode is. And evaluation is a cross-functional loop — annotation by non-engineers is part of the signal, not a QA afterthought.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It separates detection (alerting on pass-rate drop, latency, cost) from diagnosis (reading graded failure reasons), which implies two distinct instrumentation outputs and an organizational process rather than a single dashboard.

evidence_quotes.text: Vibe checks do not scale.
Without evals, you cannot detect prompt regressions, compare prompts/models objectively, or put quality gates in CI.
Changing a prompt on Monday, shipping Tuesday, and having a broken use case next week with no way to prove why.

core_insights.generalization: Any artifact changed by natural-language edits (prompts, rubrics, system messages) needs a versioned golden set plus threshold gates, or change velocity outruns defect attribution.
core_insights.insight: The argument for evals is regression economics: without an objective criterion set you cannot detect prompt regressions, compare prompts or models, or enforce CI quality gates — the failure surfaces as a use case breaking days after a prompt change with no causal trail.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It recasts evals as the missing change-management primitive for prompts/models, analogous to tests in software delivery, and motivates putting pass-rate thresholds in the deploy pipeline.

evidence_quotes.text: Every stakeholder evaluates the agent, not just engineers.
LLM-as-a-judge takes a secondary LLM to grade aspects like QA, summarization, and relevance, outputting a label and explanation.

deep_dives.research_question: What calibration procedure and agreement threshold are required before an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator can be trusted as a deployment gate?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: calibrate an LLM judge against human annotation
deep_dives.why: An uncalibrated judge creates false confidence: a pass-rate gate is only useful if judge labels track expert judgment and remain stable after judge-prompt edits.

evidence_quotes.text: Agent traces involve trees of agents, tools, and model calls where errors cascade.
Single LLM calls have one input and output span.

deep_dives.research_question: Which spans in a deep agent trace must be graded to localize failures without evaluating every span?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: What is the right granularity of span-level evaluation
deep_dives.why: Root-only grading under-attributes cascaded errors; full per-span grading scales with trace depth. A sampling or selection policy determines whether span-level evals are actionable and affordable.

evidence_quotes.text: Decision models for fast/cheap yes/no tests; code checks for JSON structure validation and regex; Rouge/BLEU for text matching.
Judge one quality per eval for LLM-as-a-judge.

deep_dives.research_question: Does routing each eval check to the lowest-cost sound grader — code/regex, small classifier, LLM judge, human — reduce cost per detected defect without reducing detection?
deep_dives.why: Single-dimension judges multiply LLM calls as quality dimensions grow; a routing policy is needed to keep eval portfolios economical.

evidence_quotes.text: Your criteria become your eval prompt.
Variable mapping connects eval inputs and outputs to exact dataset columns.

deep_dives.research_question: How should evaluator definitions bind to dataset and trace columns and be versioned so schema changes surface as explicit breakages rather than silent misgrades?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: criteria are operationalized by translating them into an eval prompt plus explicit variable mapping
deep_dives.why: The variable mapping is the interface contract; a wrong binding grades the wrong field and invalidates pass rates and gates.

evidence_quotes.text: Different eval types serve different stages from development to production.
Metrics tell you something is broken, but evals tell you what the failure mode is.

deep_dives.research_question: When production input distributions drift, how should online evaluator pass rates and labels trigger re-authoring or recalibration?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: production input distributions drift away from the dataset used to author the evaluator
deep_dives.why: Promoting an evaluator to production traffic does not guarantee it remains valid; stale evaluators can hide or invent failures.

key_claims.claim: Informal subjective testing of LLM applications does not hold up as the system and change volume grow.
key_claims.verification_question: At what prompt-change frequency or output-diversity level does subjective review measurably miss regressions that an eval suite catches?

key_claims.claim: Absent evals, teams lack regression detection, objective prompt/model comparison, and CI quality gating.
key_claims.evidence: Without evals, you cannot detect prompt regressions, compare prompts/models objectively, or put quality gates in CI.
key_claims.verification_question: Do teams with CI eval gates show lower regression escape rates than teams without them, controlling for release cadence?

key_claims.claim: Software unit tests and AI evals differ structurally: one input/one correct output with code-readable logic versus many valid outputs requiring trace inspection.
key_claims.evidence: Software tests have one input and one correct output where logic is readable in code.

key_claims.claim: Agent traces are trees of agents, tools, and model calls in which errors cascade, unlike single-span LLM calls.
key_claims.evidence: Agent traces involve trees of agents, tools, and model calls where errors cascade.
key_claims.verification_question: What fraction of agent failures originate in non-final spans, and how far do they propagate?

key_claims.claim: LLM-as-a-judge evaluators should grade exactly one quality dimension each.
key_claims.evidence: Judge one quality per eval for LLM-as-a-judge.
key_claims.verification_question: Do single-dimension judges outperform multi-dimension judges on human agreement and on stability across repeated runs?

key_claims.claim: Metrics indicate that something is broken, whereas evals identify the specific failure mode.
key_claims.evidence: Metrics tell you something is broken, but evals tell you what the failure mode is.

key_claims.claim: A natural-language criterion, once written, is directly promoted into the evaluator prompt.
key_claims.evidence: Your criteria become your eval prompt.

key_claims.claim: Different eval mechanisms are appropriate at different stages from development to production.
key_claims.evidence: Different eval types serve different stages from development to production.
key_claims.verification_question: Which eval types are cheapest per defect detected at development time versus in production monitoring?

open_questions.question: How do you validate the judge itself before trusting it as a gate — i.e., calibrate an LLM judge against human annotation and measure judge accuracy?
open_questions.research_direction: Build a labeled golden set from domain-expert annotations, measure judge–human agreement per dimension, and re-measure after every judge prompt change.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary lists annotation as an eval type and mentions every stakeholder evaluating the agent, but does not describe an agreement or calibration procedure for the judge.

open_questions.question: What is the right granularity of span-level evaluation for deep agent traces without an unacceptable cost blowup?
open_questions.research_direction: Compare root-only, sampled intermediate, and full per-span grading on identical traces for detection rate, localization accuracy, and cost.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary establishes that errors cascade across trees of spans but does not quantify evaluation cost per trace depth or propose a selection policy for which spans to grade.

open_questions.question: Does one-judge-per-quality scale economically as quality dimensions grow, or does it need a cheap-triage-then-LLM-judge cascade?
open_questions.research_direction: Prototype a tiered grader router (regex/code → small classifier → LLM judge → human) and measure cost per detected defect versus a flat LLM-judge-per-dimension baseline.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary recommends single-dimension judges and separately recommends cheap decision models, but does not give a routing or budgeting policy between them.

open_questions.question: How are online production evaluations kept stable when production input distributions drift away from the dataset used to author the evaluator?
open_questions.research_direction: Track pass-rate and label distributions of online evals over time; trigger re-authoring when disagreement with sampled human labels rises.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary recommends promoting evaluators to production traffic and continuous online evaluation but does not address distribution drift or evaluator staleness.

project_ideas.based_on: How do you validate the judge itself before trusting it as a gate
project_ideas.hypothesis: A judge calibrated against expert labels per dimension will reach at least 0.8 Cohen’s kappa and keep at least 0.75 after judge-prompt edits; an uncalibrated judge will not.
project_ideas.measurement: Cohen’s kappa vs expert labels, false-pass and false-fail rates, agreement delta after prompt edits.
project_ideas.name: Judge Calibration Harness
project_ideas.poc: Build three single-dimension judges for an agent scenario, collect expert annotations, measure agreement before and after calibration, then change each judge prompt and re-measure.

project_ideas.based_on: What is the right granularity of span-level evaluation for deep agent traces
project_ideas.hypothesis: A sampled span-grading policy can catch at least 80% of trace failures while using less than 30% of full per-span grading cost, whereas root-only grading localizes less than 50% of failures.
project_ideas.measurement: Failure detection rate, localization accuracy, eval cost per trace, cost per detected defect.
project_ideas.name: Span-Grading Selector
project_ideas.poc: Replay a trace set and compare root-only, sampled intermediate-span, and full per-span grading against known or injected failures.

project_ideas.hypothesis: Routing structural checks to code and binary checks to a small classifier before LLM judging cuts cost per detected defect by at least 50% with no more than 5% detection loss versus an LLM judge for every dimension.
project_ideas.measurement: Cost per detected defect, detection recall, latency, judge-call volume.
project_ideas.name: Tiered Grader Router
project_ideas.poc: Implement a router over regex and JSON checks, a small classifier, and an LLM judge; run on a fixed eval dataset and compare against flat LLM-judge-per-dimension grading.

project_ideas.based_on: Variable mapping connects eval inputs and outputs to exact dataset columns.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Schema-aware binding checks catch at least 90% of silent evaluator misbindings before execution, while manual variable mapping catches fewer.
project_ideas.measurement: Misbinding detection rate, false-positive rate, time-to-diagnose.
project_ideas.name: Evaluator Binding Linter
project_ideas.poc: Define evaluator templates with typed bindings to dataset and trace columns; mutate schemas and column mappings to test detection.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: SallyAnn DeLucia
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: How to write, build, and run AI evaluations (evals) for LLMs and AI agents
  • Purpose: To provide engineers and product builders with a practical guide and recipe for defining, writing, and executing AI evaluations, moving away from subjective vibe checks. SallyAnn DeLucia, Head of Product at Arize AI, presents a workshop on how to write effective AI evaluations (evals) for LLMs and agents. She contrasts 'vibe checks' with systematic evaluation, explains why traditional software unit testing falls short for AI agents, outlines types of evals (such as LLM-as-a-judge, code/logic, annotations, user feedback), provides a step-by-step recipe for writing concrete eval criteria, and walks through a live hands-on lab using Arize AX.

Topic Map

Introduction and Objectives

  • Explanation: Introduction of the speaker, Arize AI background, and three core objectives: clear definition of an eval, writing your own criteria for a real agent scenario, and building a working judge in Arize AX.
  • Key claims:
    • Evals are the primary signal for AI agents.
  • Examples:
    • Building AI agent Alex into the Arize platform.
  • Terminology:
    • evals
    • Arize AX
  • Why it matters: Establishes a foundational mental model that evals are non-negotiable for shipping reliable AI.

The Vibe Checks Problem

  • Explanation: Why informal testing ('vibe checks') fails at scale when prompts are modified and shipped without objective success criteria.
  • Key claims:
    • Vibe checks do not scale.
    • Without evals, you cannot detect prompt regressions, compare prompts/models objectively, or put quality gates in CI.
  • Examples:
    • Changing a prompt on Monday, shipping Tuesday, and having a broken use case next week with no way to prove why.
  • Terminology:
    • vibe checks
    • prompt regressions
    • quality gates
  • Why it matters: Highlights the engineering risks of deploying LLM applications without systematic testing.

Software Tests vs. AI Evals

  • Explanation: Comparing traditional software unit tests (single input, single correct output, readable logic in code) with AI agent evals (multiple valid outputs, complex downstream traces).
  • Key claims:
    • Software tests have one input and one correct output where logic is readable in code.
    • AI agents have many valid outputs and require traces to inspect multi-step logic.
  • Examples:
    • Comparing assert total(cart) == 42.00 with evaluating a travel itinerary agent.
  • Terminology:
    • unit test
    • traces
    • logs
  • Why it matters: Explains why AI testing requires new paradigms beyond standard assert statements.

Why Agents Make Evals Harder

  • Explanation: Examining agent traces—trees of LLM calls, tool calls, and retriever steps—and how error cascades make debugging and evaluation complex.
  • Key claims:
    • Single LLM calls have one input and output span.
    • Agent traces involve trees of agents, tools, and model calls where errors cascade.
  • Examples:
    • TripAgentGraph showing research agent, tool calls, vector store retriever, and chat OpenAI spans.
  • Terminology:
    • traces
    • spans
    • root span
    • tool calls
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates why observability and tracing are prerequisites for evaluating complex agentic workflows.

Types of Evals

  • Explanation: Overview of evaluation methodologies across development and production: LLM-as-a-judge, decision models, code/logic checks, annotations, agent-as-a-judge, user feedback, and business metrics.
  • Key claims:
    • LLM-as-a-judge takes a secondary LLM to grade aspects like QA, summarization, and relevance, outputting a label and explanation.
    • Different eval types serve different stages from development to production.
  • Examples:
    • Decision models for fast/cheap yes/no tests; code checks for JSON structure validation and regex; Rouge/BLEU for text matching.
  • Terminology:
    • LLM-as-a-judge
    • decision models
    • code/logic evals
    • annotations
    • agent-as-a-judge
  • Why it matters: Provides a comprehensive taxonomy of evaluation tools available to AI engineers.

Step 1: Look Before You Measure (Getting into the Lab)

  • Explanation: Practical setup instructions for logging into Arize AX, adding an AI provider API key, and opening the travel agent demo project and traces.
  • Key claims:
    • You need observability and traces before you can write effective evals.
  • Examples:
    • Logging into app.arize.com and exploring the arize-demo-llm-travel-agent project.
  • Terminology:
    • Arize AX
    • AI provider
    • traces
  • Why it matters: Brings theory into practice by guiding users through hands-on platform interaction.

Step 2: Define What 'Good' Means

  • Explanation: Moving from vague criteria (helpful, accurate, good response) to concrete criteria (answers follow-up first, matches requested days, keeps totals within budget).
  • Key claims:
    • Vague criteria fail; concrete criteria succeed.
    • Judge one quality per eval for LLM-as-a-judge.
    • Start small with one eval and iterate over time.
  • Examples:
    • Evaluating a travel planning agent for Marrakech or Prague.
  • Terminology:
    • vague vs. concrete criteria
    • rubric
    • instruction-following
  • Why it matters: Teaches the crucial skill of prompt engineering for evaluation rubrics.

Step 3: Turn Criteria Into an Evaluator

  • Explanation: Writing an LLM-as-a-judge prompt in the Arize Playground, setting up pass/fail bullet points, variable mapping, and testing the evaluator against datasets.
  • Key claims:
    • Your criteria become your eval prompt.
    • Variable mapping connects eval inputs and outputs to exact dataset columns.
  • Examples:
    • Creating an 'Output Accuracy' evaluator using GPT-4.1-mini and testing it in the Playground.
  • Terminology:
    • playground
    • evaluator template
    • variable mapping
    • dataset
  • Why it matters: Provides a complete end-to-end workflow for creating and running automated LLM judges.

The Eval Loop and Next Steps

  • Explanation: The full eval lifecycle—instrument, eval, signal, fix, deploy, monitor—and what teams should do next: annotation, promotion to production traffic, and tracking pass rates.
  • Key claims:
    • Every stakeholder evaluates the agent, not just engineers.
    • Metrics tell you something is broken, but evals tell you what the failure mode is.
  • Examples:
    • Setting up continuous online evaluations in production.
  • Terminology:
    • eval loop
    • signal
    • alignment
    • failure mode
  • Why it matters: Frames evaluation as a continuous organizational loop rather than a one-time task.

Key Points

Vibe checks do not scale

  • Explanation: Relying on subjective feel when changing prompts leads to undetected regressions and broken use cases in production.
  • Evidence: Week-later failures after prompt tweaks with no way to prove why.
  • Practical implication: Teams must adopt systematic evaluations and quality gates in CI before shipping AI agents.

Software tests differ fundamentally from AI evals

  • Explanation: Traditional unit tests check single inputs against single hardcoded outputs with visible code logic, whereas LLMs have multiple valid outputs and opaque execution traces.
  • Evidence: Comparison between assert statements and multi-criteria travel itinerary evaluations.
  • Practical implication: AI engineering requires tracing execution paths and utilizing LLM-as-a-judge for probabilistic outputs.

Judge one quality per eval

  • Explanation: LLM judges perform poorly when asked to evaluate multiple complex dimensions simultaneously; focus each evaluator on a single concrete quality.
  • Evidence: Research on LLM-as-a-judge performance when handling single vs. multi-criteria rubrics.
  • Practical implication: Start with one narrow eval (e.g., instruction-following or groundedness) and add more over time.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Eval Criteria Framework

  • How it works: Structured method for writing concrete evaluation prompts by defining task, success, failure, judging quality, and pass/fail conditions.
  • Components:
    • Task (one line description)
    • Success (one sentence)
    • Failure (one sentence)
    • Judging quality (e.g., relevance, instruction-following)
    • Pass when (up to 3 bullets)
    • Fail when (up to 3 bullets)
  • When to use: When designing new LLM-as-a-judge evaluators.

The Eval Loop

  • How it works: Continuous operational cycle for managing AI quality across development and production.
  • Components:
    • Instrument
    • Eval
    • Signal
    • Fix
    • Deploy
    • Monitor
  • When to use: When implementing production AI observability and testing pipelines.

Examples & Case Studies

A travel planning agent receives a user request for a 3-day trip to Prague with an $800 budget and a local, non-touristy vibe.

  • Illustrates: Multi-step agent trace execution including research agents, tool calls, and LLM summarization.
  • Lesson: Agents require inspection of intermediate tool outputs and final itineraries to evaluate correctness.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Stop relying solely on vibe checks when updating prompts.
    • Write concrete, specific success and failure criteria instead of vague labels like 'helpful'.
    • Isolate one quality per LLM judge eval.
  • Strategic:
    • Integrate evals into CI/CD pipelines as automated quality gates.
    • Involve cross-functional stakeholders (product, support, domain experts) in defining agent success.
    • Build an iterative eval loop that scales from development datasets to continuous production monitoring.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • Which agent span (root, tool, or retriever) is most critical to evaluate first?
    • How do decision models compare to full LLM-as-a-judge setups for our specific use case?
    • How can we align human feedback data with automated eval pass rates in production?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • LLM-as-a-judge performs better when handling only one evaluation criterion at a time rather than multiple criteria simultaneously. (empirical)
  • OpenAI released their decision model API around October 2026. (factual temporal)

Notable Quotes

"Evals are the primary signal for agents — ours included." (at 0:12) "Traces= logs for AI. Evals= tests for AI." (at 5:56) "Metrics let you something broke. Evals tell you which failure mode." (at 55:50)

Compressed Summary

  • Vibe checks fail to scale because they cannot prove prompt regression or objectify model upgrades.
  • AI agent evaluation requires tracing multi-step execution graphs rather than simple unit tests.
  • LLM-as-a-judge evaluators should focus on a single concrete quality per prompt rubric.
  • Arize AX provides tracing, playground testing, and variable mapping to operationalize the eval loop.
  • Keywords: evals, llm-as-a-judge, traces, agents, observability
  • Core insight: Systematic, concrete evaluations are essential to replace subjective vibe checks and reliably ship AI agents from development to production.

- **Explanation**: Why informal testing ('vibe checks') fails at scale when prompts are modified and shipped without objective success criteria.
- **Key claims**:
  - Vibe checks do not scale.
  - Without evals, you cannot detect prompt regressions, compare prompts/models objectively, or put quality gates in CI.
- **Examples**:
  - Changing a prompt on Monday, shipping Tuesday, and having a broken use case next week with no way to prove why.
- **Terminology**:
  - vibe checks
  - prompt regressions
  - quality gates
- **Why it matters**: Highlights the engineering risks of deploying LLM applications without systematic testing.
### Software Tests vs. AI Evals
- **Explanation**: Comparing traditional software unit tests (single input, single correct output, readable logic in code) with AI agent evals (multiple valid outputs, complex downstream traces).
- **Key claims**:
  - Software tests have one input and one correct output where logic is readable in code.
  - AI agents have many valid outputs and require traces to inspect multi-step logic.
- **Examples**:
  - Comparing assert total(cart) == 42.00 with evaluating a travel itinerary agent.
- **Terminology**:
  - unit test
  - traces
  - logs
- **Why it matters**: Explains why AI testing requires new paradigms beyond standard assert statements.
### Why Agents Make Evals Harder
- **Explanation**: Examining agent traces—trees of LLM calls, tool calls, and retriever steps—and how error cascades make debugging and evaluation complex.
- **Key claims**:
  - Single LLM calls have one input and output span.
  - Agent traces involve trees of agents, tools, and model calls where errors cascade.
- **Examples**:
  - TripAgentGraph showing research agent, tool calls, vector store retriever, and chat OpenAI spans.
- **Terminology**:
  - traces
  - spans
  - root span
  - tool calls
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates why observability and tracing are prerequisites for evaluating complex agentic workflows.
### Types of Evals
- **Explanation**: Overview of evaluation methodologies across development and production: LLM-as-a-judge, decision models, code/logic checks, annotations, agent-as-a-judge, user feedback, and business metrics.
- **Key claims**:
  - LLM-as-a-judge takes a secondary LLM to grade aspects like QA, summarization, and relevance, outputting a label and explanation.
  - Different eval types serve different stages from development to production.
- **Examples**:
  - Decision models for fast/cheap yes/no tests; code checks for JSON structure validation and regex; Rouge/BLEU for text matching.
- **Terminology**:
  - LLM-as-a-judge
  - decision models
  - code/logic evals
  - annotations
  - agent-as-a-judge
- **Why it matters**: Provides a comprehensive taxonomy of evaluation tools available to AI engineers.
### Step 1: Look Before You Measure (Getting into the Lab)
- **Explanation**: Practical setup instructions for logging into Arize AX, adding an AI provider API key, and opening the travel agent demo project and traces.
- **Key claims**:
  - You need observability and traces before you can write effective evals.
- **Examples**:
  - Logging into app.arize.com and exploring the arize-demo-llm-travel-agent project.
- **Terminology**:
  - Arize AX
  - AI provider
  - traces
- **Why it matters**: Brings theory into practice by guiding users through hands-on platform interaction.
### Step 2: Define What 'Good' Means
- **Explanation**: Moving from vague criteria (helpful, accurate, good response) to concrete criteria (answers follow-up first, matches requested days, keeps totals within budget).
- **Key claims**:
  - Vague criteria fail; concrete criteria succeed.
  - Judge one quality per eval for LLM-as-a-judge.
  - Start small with one eval and iterate over time.
- **Examples**:
  - Evaluating a travel planning agent for Marrakech or Prague.
- **Terminology**:
  - vague vs. concrete criteria
  - rubric
  - instruction-following
- **Why it matters**: Teaches the crucial skill of prompt engineering for evaluation rubrics.
### Step 3: Turn Criteria Into an Evaluator
- **Explanation**: Writing an LLM-as-a-judge prompt in the Arize Playground, setting up pass/fail bullet points, variable mapping, and testing the evaluator against datasets.
- **Key claims**:
  - Your criteria become your eval prompt.
  - Variable mapping connects eval inputs and outputs to exact dataset columns.
- **Examples**:
  - Creating an 'Output Accuracy' evaluator using GPT-4.1-mini and testing it in the Playground.
- **Terminology**:
  - playground
  - evaluator template
  - variable mapping
  - dataset
- **Why it matters**: Provides a complete end-to-end workflow for creating and running automated LLM judges.
### The Eval Loop and Next Steps
- **Explanation**: The full eval lifecycle—instrument, eval, signal, fix, deploy, monitor—and what teams should do next: annotation, promotion to production traffic, and tracking pass rates.
- **Key claims**:
  - Every stakeholder evaluates the agent, not just engineers.
  - Metrics tell you something is broken, but evals tell you what the failure mode is.
- **Examples**:
  - Setting up continuous online evaluations in production.
- **Terminology**:
  - eval loop
  - signal
  - alignment
  - failure mode
- **Why it matters**: Frames evaluation as a continuous organizational loop rather than a one-time task.
## Key Points
### Vibe checks do not scale
- **Explanation**: Relying on subjective feel when changing prompts leads to undetected regressions and broken use cases in production.
- **Evidence**: Week-later failures after prompt tweaks with no way to prove why.
- **Practical implication**: Teams must adopt systematic evaluations and quality gates in CI before shipping AI agents.
### Software tests differ fundamentally from AI evals
- **Explanation**: Traditional unit tests check single inputs against single hardcoded outputs with visible code logic, whereas LLMs have multiple valid outputs and opaque execution traces.
- **Evidence**: Comparison between assert statements and multi-criteria travel itinerary evaluations.
- **Practical implication**: AI engineering requires tracing execution paths and utilizing LLM-as-a-judge for probabilistic outputs.
### Judge one quality per eval
- **Explanation**: LLM judges perform poorly when asked to evaluate multiple complex dimensions simultaneously; focus each evaluator on a single concrete quality.
- **Evidence**: Research on LLM-as-a-judge performance when handling single vs. multi-criteria rubrics.
- **Practical implication**: Start with one narrow eval (e.g., instruction-following or groundedness) and add more over time.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Eval Criteria Framework
- **How it works**: Structured method for writing concrete evaluation prompts by defining task, success, failure, judging quality, and pass/fail conditions.
- **Components**:
  - Task (one line description)
  - Success (one sentence)
  - Failure (one sentence)
  - Judging quality (e.g., relevance, instruction-following)
  - Pass when (up to 3 bullets)
  - Fail when (up to 3 bullets)
- **When to use**: When designing new LLM-as-a-judge evaluators.
### The Eval Loop
- **How it works**: Continuous operational cycle for managing AI quality across development and production.
- **Components**:
  - Instrument
  - Eval
  - Signal
  - Fix
  - Deploy
  - Monitor
- **When to use**: When implementing production AI observability and testing pipelines.
## Examples & Case Studies
### A travel planning agent receives a user request for a 3-day trip to Prague with an $800 budget and a local, non-touristy vibe.
- **Illustrates**: Multi-step agent trace execution including research agents, tool calls, and LLM summarization.
- **Lesson**: Agents require inspection of intermediate tool outputs and final itineraries to evaluate correctness.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Stop relying solely on vibe checks when updating prompts.
  - Write concrete, specific success and failure criteria instead of vague labels like 'helpful'.
  - Isolate one quality per LLM judge eval.
- **Strategic**:
  - Integrate evals into CI/CD pipelines as automated quality gates.
  - Involve cross-functional stakeholders (product, support, domain experts) in defining agent success.
  - Build an iterative eval loop that scales from development datasets to continuous production monitoring.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - Which agent span (root, tool, or retriever) is most critical to evaluate first?
  - How do decision models compare to full LLM-as-a-judge setups for our specific use case?
  - How can we align human feedback data with automated eval pass rates in production?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- LLM-as-a-judge performs better when handling only one evaluation criterion at a time rather than multiple criteria simultaneously. (empirical)
- OpenAI released their decision model API around October 2026. (factual temporal)
## Notable Quotes
> "Evals are the primary signal for agents — ours included." (at 0:12)
> "Traces= logs for AI. Evals= tests for AI." (at 5:56)
> "Metrics let you something broke. Evals tell you which failure mode." (at 55:50)
## Compressed Summary
- Vibe checks fail to scale because they cannot prove prompt regression or objectify model upgrades.
- AI agent evaluation requires tracing multi-step execution graphs rather than simple unit tests.
- LLM-as-a-judge evaluators should focus on a single concrete quality per prompt rubric.
- Arize AX provides tracing, playground testing, and variable mapping to operationalize the eval loop.
- **Keywords**: evals, llm-as-a-judge, traces, agents, observability
- **Core insight**: Systematic, concrete evaluations are essential to replace subjective vibe checks and reliably ship AI agents from development to production.
